To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the pattern induced orientation of flies can be explained in terms of a simple model of the fly's visual system.

the orientation of a flying insect towards a pattern is a stochastic process, that the probability distribution of the orientation is a stationary process, and that the stationary orientation probability is a functional of the pattern's torque distribution.
the fly's eye is a “superposition eye” and that the pattern preference of the fixed flying fly is a result of the interaction between the pattern's attractiveness and a noise process.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the visual orientation behaviour in fixed flying flies (musca domestica), in response to simple patterns.

a quantitative description of the visual orientation behaviour in fixed flies, and we have found that the “attracting” and “repelling” properties of the patterns are due to an interaction between the visual system and the motor system of the fly.
the study of the visual orientation behaviour (in the laboratory) of fixed flying insects.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the pattern-induced flight orientation of the housefly is a complex phenomenon, which can be explained by a combination of a number of elementary mechanisms, such as: a) the “superposition” of elementary responses to single stripes; b) the “early symmetry breaking”, which is caused by the correlation in the input signal; c) inhibitory interactions between channels.

a phenomenological description of the visual orientation behaviour towards elementary patterns is possible in terms of the superposition principle and of a shift in the D(ψ) profile, but only if the inhibitory interactions are properly taken into account.
the phenomenological model presented in the preceding paper (Poggio and Reichhardt, 1973a) provides an adequate description of the pattern-induced orientation behaviour of the fly.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the pattern orientation behaviour of fixed flies can be described by a simple theory which is based on the following assumptions: (i) the visual system of the fly is linear and shift-invariant; (ii) the visual system is a low-pass filter; (iii) the system is a spatial filter with a Gaussian spatial impulse response; (iv) the system is sensitive to a small number of spatial frequencies (about 4) and (v) the system is insensitive to the direction of the stimulus.
the phenomenological theory is a good first approximation, but that the quantitative aspects of the pattern induced orientation behaviour require a more detailed analysis of the visual system.

the phenomenological theory of Poggio and Riechardt (1972) is essentially correct, but that the quantitative predictions of the theory have to be corrected in order to take into account the inhibitory interactions between the channels.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the pattern induced orientation behaviour of flies can be described as a “biased random walk” in a space of orientations.
the pattern induced flight behaviour of the housefly can be described by the same phenomenological model as that proposed by Reichardt (1961).

, although a number of important problems remain unsolved, we have a fairly good understanding of the basic mechanism of the fly's pattern induced orientation behaviour, at least for the case of elementary patterns.
